2. The authors show MOFS retention in ileum, cecum, and colon, but it remains unclear
whether this distribution relates to local pH, mucus viscosity, or motility. A brief
mechanistic discussion or supporting experiment is suggested.
Response: Thank you for the insightful comment. In the revised manuscript, we have
made a further discussion on the potential influences of local pH, mucus viscosity, and
motility on MOFS retention. Corresponding discussion has been added in the revised
manuscript (Page 7, Line 30 and Page 8, Line 1-5; Page 9, Line 10-13): MMT is a clay
containing multiple isomeric substituents, where the aluminum and silicon atoms at the
crystal edges undergo partial hydrolysis in water, forming silanol and aluminum
hydroxyl groups (Proc Natl Acad Sci USA 2024, 121, e2320482121; Nat Chem 2023,
15, 119-128). These unsaturated edge sites are more reactive than saturated base sites
and can bind to mucin in the mucus layer of the intestinal wall through hydrogen
bonding, van der Waals forces, and hydrophobic interactions. Give MMT is known to
bind mucin in the mucus layer, the differential retention of MMT@Bac@TL across gut
segments might be resulted from the structural and thickness variations in the mucus
layer (Immunol Rev 2014, 260, 8-20). Additionally, pH gradients along the
gastrointestinal tract and gut motility could also play a role by influencing the binding
(Small 2025, 21, 2410258).
3. Please include more detailed time-course measurements of tryptophan and lactulose
levels in intestinal contents to support claims of sustained release in vivo.
Response: Thank you for the suggestion. Accordingly, we have further measured
tryptophan and lactulose levels in intestinal contents after 24 and 48 hours of oral
administration. Corresponding results have been added in the revised manuscript (Page
10, Line 17-30): Moreover, we monitored the metabolites over a time course. The
concentration of indole in the MMT@Bac@TL group was increased by ~1.4-fold
compared to those in the Bac and MMT@Bac group 24 hours after oral administration,
respectively (Supplementary Fig. 4a). Indole level at 48 hours after oral administration
and lactate levels at 24 hours and 48 hours showed no significant differences
(Supplementary Fig. 4b-d). Notably, both the levels of indole and lactic acid in the
MMT@Bac@TL group were increased by ~2-fold compared to the Bac group 72 hours
after oral gavage. In contrast, the administration of MMT@Bac failed to enhance lactic
acid production throughout the time course (Fig. 3g and h). These dynamic changes in
indole and lactic acid productions observed over time in the MMT@Bac@TL group
might be associated with transitions, substrate availability, and microbial adaptation of
the sample in the gut. Collectively, these data showed that MMT@Bac@TL enabled
long-lasting in situ biosynthesis in the intestine, and that the production of beneficial
metabolites could be amplified by co-loading tryptophan and lactulose.

4. While IL-1β, VEGF, and TGF-β were assessed, additional pro-inflammatory

Response: Thank you for your valuable suggestion. Based on this suggestion, we have
supplemented additional cytokines and epithelial integrity metrics. Corresponding
results have been added in the revised manuscript (Page 15, Line 17-24; Page 17, Line

compared to the medium group, contributing to an increased ratio of IL-4 to IL-6

Nat Rev Gastroenterol Hepatol 2023, 20, 538-553). In contrast, increases in IL-6 and
NO are commonly involved in the aggravation of immunopathology during gut
inflammation (Inflamm Bowel Dis 2007, 13, 1016-1023; Front Endocrinol 2024, 15,
1390351).

5. Although MOFS reduces Candida albicans, the mechanistic basis is only partially
explained.
Response: We thank the reviewer for offering the constructive suggestions. The relevant
discussion has been supplemented in the revised manuscript (Page 20, Line 4-9). In
addition to its role against pathogen infection, indole offers a viable alternative to
eliminate C. albicans and its biofilms (J Appl Microbiol 2012, 113, 622-628). Lactic
acid-producing bacteria are known to block C. albicans filamentation, an important
virulence trait, by affecting the intestinal microenvironment (Gut Pathog 2023, 15, 30).
Additionally, E. faecalis was identified as secreting Fsr-dependent proteases, which
inhibit hyphal morphogenesis and biofilm formation in the fungus, thereby reducing
the virulence (J Appl Microbiol 2012, 113, 622-628).

studies, a benchmark group using a clinically available probiotic should be included to

advantages of MOFS, we have added a benchmark comparison with the clinically
available probiotics EcN and Bacillus subtilis (Bs) in the revised manuscript.

including EcN and Bacillus subtilis (Bs). C. albicans were co-cultured with EcN, Bs or
MMT@Bac@TL in yeast extract peptone dextrose (YPD) medium at a ratio of 1:10.

cells treated with culture medium served as the control. As shown in Supplementary
Fig. 17c, the ratio of M2 to M1 macrophages was over 4-fold increase in
MMT@Bac@TL compared to other treatments, indicating a potent anti-inflammatory
effect of MMT@Bac@TL.
